Pregnancy

Fetal position and sex testing: what can tell you about your baby?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A baby’s position in the womb cannot reliably tell you whether they are a boy or a girl. Some prenatal tests can provide sex information, but their main purposes, timing, risks and limits are different.

A baby’s position does not tell you their sex

There is no reliable rule that a boy lies vertically, stays on a particular side or moves differently from a girl. Babies change position repeatedly, especially earlier in pregnancy. A head-down, breech or sideways position describes how the baby is lying, not their sex.

Position can nevertheless affect a scan: if the legs are closed or the relevant anatomy is hidden, the sonographer may not obtain a clear view. That is a limitation of the image, not evidence for one sex. The position seen at one appointment may also be different at the next.

Some parents want to know during pregnancy and others prefer a surprise. Both choices are reasonable. Tell the maternity team your preference before a scan or genetic test, including whether you want sex information kept out of a result discussion when possible.

Separate sex information from a baby’s health assessment

Ultrasound examines physical structures, while genetic tests examine selected DNA or chromosome information. These are different kinds of evidence. Neither a prediction of external genital appearance nor a chromosome result provides a complete description of a child’s health, future personality or gender identity.

Screening estimates the chance of particular conditions; diagnostic testing can establish whether a condition being tested for is present. A low-chance screening result does not exclude every genetic or structural condition, and a higher-chance result usually needs a discussion about confirmation.

Before choosing a test, ask what it looks for, what it cannot show and what an unexpected result would mean. If the reason is a family history of a sex-linked condition, specialist genetic counselling is more useful than arranging a commercial sex-prediction test without advice.

Ultrasound can sometimes show the external genitalia

During a medical ultrasound, sound waves create images that help assess growth, anatomy and the placenta. When the genital area is clearly visible, its appearance may allow the sonographer to offer an opinion about fetal sex. An unclear image should be described as unclear rather than turned into a confident guess.

Early predictions, including those made around twelve weeks, are less dependable than a suitable view later in pregnancy. In England, the routine mid-pregnancy screening scan is usually at eighteen to twenty-one weeks; timing varies elsewhere. The health examination is the priority, and disclosure depends on local practice.

The examiner considers several views and the stage of development. A protrusion or a few parallel lines in a still image is not a dependable do-it-yourself test. Even later scans cannot promise complete certainty, and the team may be unable to tell you at that appointment.

Skull shape and the side of the placenta are not substitutes

Online prediction methods often assign sex according to the shape of the forehead or skull. Another, commonly called the Ramzi method, uses the side on which the developing placenta appears. These are not established clinical methods for determining fetal sex.

An ultrasound photograph is a selected view, and its orientation is not something a viewer can safely infer from a screenshot alone. A medical statement about placental location has a different purpose from a claim that right means boy or left means girl. Do not use either claim to contradict a clinical assessment.

The same caution applies to the baby’s lie, abdominal shape and other traditional guesses. They can be discussed as guesses, but they should not determine care or provide reassurance about a possible inherited condition. If certainty matters medically, ask which test can answer that specific question.

NIPT analyses DNA fragments in a blood sample

Non-invasive prenatal testing, also called cell-free DNA screening, uses a blood sample from the pregnant person. Most DNA fragments in that sample are maternal; a smaller proportion comes from the placenta and usually reflects the baby’s chromosome information. It is not a direct sample of every fetal cell.

Testing is commonly available from ten weeks, depending on the service. It is used primarily to screen for selected chromosome conditions, especially trisomies 21, 18 and 13. Some panels also report sex information. Screening for sex-chromosome conditions such as Turner syndrome is a separate choice that deserves counselling rather than being treated as an automatic extra.

When a laboratory offers fetal-sex reporting, it interprets chromosome signals, including Y-chromosome material, under its validated criteria. Absence of a Y signal in an inadequate or failed sample is not proof of a female result. Ask what the laboratory actually reported instead of interpreting raw wording yourself.

A blood test result is not a 100% guarantee

NIPT is a highly effective screening tool for some conditions, but it can produce a false-positive, false-negative or inconclusive result. Performance differs by condition and pregnancy circumstances. A statement about accuracy for Down syndrome cannot simply be applied to every additional result on a panel.

A no-call result means the laboratory could not provide a usable answer. It is not a reassuring negative and should not be used to predict sex. Your team should discuss the reason, the pregnancy findings and options such as further ultrasound, another sample or diagnostic testing; repeating the blood test is not always the best next step.

If blood-test and scan information differ, avoid deciding which is right from internet comparisons. Bring both reports to the maternity team or a genetic counsellor. The explanation may require review of the test, the pregnancy and the anatomy. Do not make an irreversible pregnancy decision from an unconfirmed screening result.

Amniocentesis tests cells from the fluid around the baby

Amniocentesis involves passing a thin needle through the abdomen under ultrasound guidance to collect a small amount of amniotic fluid. Cells and material in the sample are tested for the specific chromosome or genetic conditions agreed with the team. It is usually performed from fifteen weeks; NHS information gives a typical window of fifteen to twenty weeks, with later testing possible.

The result may include sex-chromosome information, but the purpose is diagnosis of a medical question, not simply satisfying curiosity. The procedure is not routinely used solely to learn sex. It can give a much firmer answer about a tested condition than screening, without guaranteeing that every possible condition has been excluded.

Risks include miscarriage, infection and fluid leakage, and some people have cramping or bleeding afterward. Ask about the centre’s risk estimate and your circumstances. Seek urgent maternity advice after the procedure for persistent or severe pain, vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, fever or contractions. Follow the team’s aftercare instructions.

CVS takes a sample of the placenta earlier in pregnancy

Chorionic villus sampling, or CVS, tests a small piece of placental tissue. A specialist obtains it through the abdomen with a needle or, in selected circumstances, through the cervix. NHS information describes a usual window of eleven to fourteen weeks, although the exact timing depends on the service and clinical situation.

Like amniocentesis, CVS is offered to investigate particular genetic or chromosome concerns after discussion of benefits, limits and alternatives. It may reveal sex-chromosome information, but it is not a routine sex-disclosure procedure. You can accept or decline it after counselling.

CVS carries risks including miscarriage and infection. Sometimes results need further interpretation or another test, including amniocentesis. A rapid result is not necessarily the full set of results. Ask which answers are ready, what remains pending and whom to contact if you have concerning symptoms after sampling.

IVF with embryo testing happens before embryo transfer

In vitro fertilisation creates embryos outside the body. Preimplantation genetic testing, or PGT, may then examine sampled cells before an embryo is transferred to the uterus. IVF by itself does not provide a genetic sex result; testing is a separate part of the process.

Some forms of PGT can report sex-chromosome information, and testing may be relevant when avoiding a particular inherited condition. Using it for nonmedical sex selection involves separate ethical, legal and clinic-policy questions. Availability should be checked locally rather than assumed from a clinic advertisement in another country.

This is not a way to test or change the sex of an established pregnancy. IVF involves medicines, egg collection, time, expense and medical risks. Testing is not infallible, and there may be no suitable embryo of a preferred sex or no resulting pregnancy. A promise of a guaranteed baby is not a realistic description of the treatment.

Choose the next step with clear expectations

For most parents who are simply curious, it is reasonable to ask whether the routine scan can provide an opinion and to accept that the answer may remain uncertain. Extra procedures are not automatically needed because a baby’s position prevented a view.

If a screening result, family history or scan finding creates a medical concern, ask for a discussion of the available diagnostic options. Useful questions include: What exactly is being tested? When can it be done? What are the risks? Could it fail to give an answer? Will I receive sex information even if I do not want it?

Write down your preferences and ask how results will be communicated. A result may arrive in stages, and different reports may answer different questions. Clear counselling helps you make an informed choice without treating a position, photograph or commercial claim as a complete assessment of your baby.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Fetal lie, skull shape and placenta-side guesses are not established sex-testing methods.

NIPT is screening, and inconclusive or conflicting results need follow-up.

Diagnostic sampling and IVF with PGT are distinct procedures with specific indications and limitations.

How BeMama can help

Decide what information you want, ask what each test can answer and keep the actual reports for a discussion with your maternity team.

When to seek help

After invasive testing, obtain urgent maternity advice for bleeding, fluid leakage, fever, contractions or persistent severe pain. Do not make irreversible decisions from an unconfirmed screening result.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Position affects the view, not the baby’s sex.
  • Ultrasound cannot always provide a clear or certain answer.
  • A no-call NIPT result is not a negative result.
  • CVS and amniocentesis investigate medical questions and carry risks.
  • IVF with PGT does not guarantee a pregnancy or a baby of a preferred sex.

Frequently asked questions

Does a boy usually lie vertically in the womb?

No reliable clinical rule links a vertical position with male sex. Babies change position, and their lie cannot determine sex.

Can the placenta being on the right tell me it is a boy?

No. Placenta-side methods such as the Ramzi method are not established clinical sex tests.

Can a twelve-week scan give a certain answer?

No. Early external genital appearances and limited views make prediction uncertain. Ask the sonographer what can reasonably be concluded.

Why could the sonographer not tell me at the later scan?

The baby’s position or the available view may hide the genital area. Hospital disclosure policies also differ; the medical examination remains the priority.

Is NIPT completely accurate from ten weeks?

No. Ten weeks is a common starting point, not a guarantee of perfect accuracy. NIPT remains a screening test with possible incorrect or inconclusive results.

Does a no-call result mean the baby is a girl?

No. It means the laboratory could not give a usable result. Ask your maternity team about counselling and appropriate follow-up.

Are CVS and amniocentesis just earlier sex tests?

No. They are invasive diagnostic procedures used to answer specific medical questions, with risks and limits that need discussion.

Can IVF change the sex of a pregnancy I already have?

No. Embryo testing associated with IVF occurs before transfer and does not change an established pregnancy.

What if the scan and blood test give different information?

Bring both reports to your maternity team or genetic counsellor. They can review the circumstances and decide whether further assessment is useful.

Can I choose not to find out the sex?

Yes. Tell the team before testing and ask how your preference can be recorded and respected when reports are discussed.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
